traits: Lawn browns in patches seemingly overnight, uniform across a large area
Light-colored, inverted "Y" mark on the front of the dark head
Caterpillars feed in groups, advancing across turf like a front
Birds suddenly very interested in the lawn — they find them first

look_alikes.difference: Fall armyworm has an inverted "Y" on the head and damages turf uniformly; sod webworm larvae are smaller with patchy, notched blades.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the caterpillar's head marking, plus a wide shot of the damage pattern.

copy.what_it_means: Despite the name, fall armyworms damage Florida turf in both spring and fall. The name is literal — they advance across the lawn in fronts, eating as they go, and the birds usually find them before you do.
copy.fact: The name is literal — they advance across turf in fronts, eating as they go.
copy.blurb: Fast movers. The birds found them before you did.

tech_notes: Confirm inverted Y head marking. Soap-flush or visual count at dusk; treat while larvae are small for best control.

traits: Small tan moths flush up in a zigzag pattern when you walk through or mow the lawn
Grass blades notched and chewed, patches look scalped
Cream larvae with brown-spotted segments, up to about 11 mm
Damage appears fast in late summer and fall, with adults present year-round in south Florida

look_alikes.difference: Sod webworm damage starts as ragged, notched blades in smaller patches; fall armyworm eats uniformly across a large area and has an inverted "Y" on the head.
look_alikes.next_photo: A wide shot of the damage pattern, plus a close-up of any caterpillar found.

copy.what_it_means: The moths do zero damage — it's their caterpillars feeding at night that shear the lawn. This is a late-summer classic; a technician can evaluate how far the damage has spread and whether the lawn needs overseeding to recover.
copy.fact: The moths do zero damage — it’s their caterpillars feeding at night that shear the lawn.
copy.blurb: Late-summer classic. A technician evaluates the extent of the damage and the best path to recovery.

tech_notes: Moths flush when disturbed; larvae feed at night (window-feeding first 4 instars, then full blade). Treat late afternoon; re-check 10-14 days.

safety_line: The most venomous caterpillar in the US — hidden spines under the fur cause intense pain. Never touch it. See a doctor if pain or swelling worsens. Call 911 if someone has trouble breathing.
traits: Looks like a tiny blonde toupee — completely furry, teardrop-shaped, about 2.5 cm
Head hidden beneath dense hair; a short tail extends past the body
Found on oaks, elms, and citrus; sometimes drops onto railings or shoulders
Fall is peak season in Southwest Florida

look_alikes.difference: Puss caterpillars are uniformly fuzzy with no visible spines; Io moth caterpillars are bright green with a red-and-white stripe and obvious branched spines.
look_alikes.next_photo: From a few feet away, zoom in on the body surface without touching it — fuzzy all over versus spiny with visible stripes.

copy.what_it_means: The most venomous caterpillar in the United States hides under that soft-looking fur — the "hairs" conceal venomous spines. Teach kids the "cute means don’t touch" rule; stings are intensely painful but rarely dangerous.
copy.fact: The most venomous caterpillar in the United States hides under that fur — the "hairs" conceal venomous spines.
copy.blurb: Never touch; teach kids the "cute = don’t" rule. Stings are intensely painful but rarely dangerous.

tech_notes: Confirm dense uniform fur, no visible spine pattern. Advise removal by trained tech (tape-lift or clipping), never bare-handed.

safety_line: Spines sting like nettles and can cause a burning, itchy welt. See a doctor for a strong allergic reaction. Call 911 if someone has trouble breathing.
traits: Bright green with a red-and-white racing stripe down each side
Branched spines covering the body, up to about 6.5 cm long
Feeds in groups on oaks, hibiscus, and many other shrubs
Grows into a moth with large false "eyes" on the hindwings

look_alikes.difference: Io moth caterpillars are green with branched spines and a red-white stripe; puss caterpillars are uniformly furry with no visible spines.
look_alikes.next_photo: From a few feet away, zoom in on the body surface without touching it — spiny with a stripe versus uniformly fuzzy.

copy.what_it_means: It grows into a moth with huge false "eyes" on its hindwings — one of Florida’s prettiest transformations from one of its spiciest caterpillars. Look, photograph, and don’t touch; pain from a sting typically fades within hours.
copy.fact: It grows into a moth with huge false "eyes" on its hindwings, used to startle predators.
copy.blurb: Spines sting like nettles. Look, photograph, don’t pet.

tech_notes: Confirm branched scoli spines + red/white lateral stripe. Advise removal by trained tech if on a high-traffic plant; no treatment usually needed.
